big: When the RBI raises the repo rate, bond prices dip first and pay more afterwards. A client who sees a small fall in a multi-asset NAV deserves an explanation before they ask for one.

h: The week after a rate hike
lines: The RBI raised the repo rate in October 2026 and my multi-asset fund's NAV is down a little. Did I make a mistake?
A small dip in the debt part is normal after a hike. Let me show you what it is, and what comes after it.

alt: Three pairs of bars comparing a longer and a shorter debt sleeve after yields rise by a quarter point
caps: Assume yields on the sleeve's bonds rise 0.25 point. Price dip is about duration times that.
A sleeve with 3 years of duration dips about 75 paise per ₹100. A 1-year sleeve dips 25 paise.
The debt sleeve is 30% of the fund, so the fund's NAV dips about 22.5 paise per ₹100.
New bonds also pay more. The 3-year sleeve earns back its dip in about 3 years.

alt: Three bars of extra yield earned over three years against a dip of 75 paise
caps: After the hike the sleeve yields 0.25 point more, on every ₹100 held.
Year 1: about 25 paise of extra yield. Year 2: 50 paise in total.
Year 3: 75 paise, the same as the dip. This is simplified, with no compounding.
A longer duration means a bigger dip and a longer wait. A shorter one dips less and recovers sooner.

h: What a rate hike does by sleeve
title: After the hike
stops: Debt: small dip, then higher accrual
Gold and equity respond to other drivers
The dip is a permanent loss of capital
alt: A shield with true and false statements about a rate hike and a multi-asset fund
caps: Each sleeve of a multi-asset fund answers to its own drivers.
Debt: a small dip now, better accrual going forward. Gold and equity react to their own news.
The dip is a mark to market change, not a permanent loss unless the bonds default or are sold low.

h: What it looks like in rupees
intro: A ₹10 lakh holding in a fund with 30% in debt of 3 years' duration.
note: Assumed numbers to show scale. A longer-duration debt sleeve dips more; check the modified duration in the factsheet.

q: After a repo rate hike, a client's multi-asset fund shows a NAV dip of about 0.2% in a week. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: The manager made a mistake in the equity part, which is the only part that moves
The fund has lost part of its capital for good, and it cannot be recovered later
Debt sleeve bonds repriced at higher yields, and now earn more from here
Gold always falls after a rate hike, so gold alone explains the whole of the dip
why: Equity is not the only part that moves. A rate hike works on the bond prices in the debt sleeve first.
A mark-to-market dip is not a permanent loss. Held, the bonds earn the higher yield from here.
Higher yields lower existing bond prices, which shows as a small dip. The bonds then accrue more than before.
Gold has no fixed reaction to a hike. The direct effect of higher yields is on bond prices in the debt sleeve.

q: A fund has 30% in debt with modified duration of 3 years. Yields on those bonds rise 0.25 point. What is the approximate dip in the fund's NAV, from the debt sleeve alone?
opts: About 0.2%, since the sleeve dips 0.75% and it is 30% of the fund
About 0.75%, since the sleeve dips by duration times the rise in yields
About 0.25%, since the NAV moves by the same amount as the yield did
About 2.25%, since the duration is multiplied by the rise and by three again
why: Sleeve dip: 3 times 0.25 is 0.75%. Fund dip: 0.75% times 30% is about 0.225%.
That is the dip of the debt sleeve itself. Only 30% of the fund sits in it, so the NAV falls less.
The yield rise and the price dip are different numbers. The dip is duration times the yield rise.
Multiplying by the duration twice overstates the dip. One multiplication gives the sleeve's move.

q: The 3-year-duration sleeve dipped 0.75% when yields rose 0.25 point. Roughly how long does the higher yield take to make up that dip?
opts: About 3 months, since new bonds pay interest every month of the year
About 12 months, since yields are quoted as a rate per year
It never makes it up, because a dip in bond prices is permanent
About 3 years, which is close to the sleeve's duration
why: Three months of extra yield is about 6 paise. It does not cover a dip of 75 paise.
One year of extra yield is 25 paise, a third of the dip. The full amount takes longer.
The dip is a mark to market change. Held, the bonds earn more, so the loss is made up over time.
Extra yield of 0.25 point a year earns back 0.75 in about 3 years. Duration works as a rough break-even time.

q: A client who saw the debt sleeve dip wants to leave the multi-asset fund altogether. What is the strongest point for the adviser to make?
opts: The manager has hedged all interest rate risk, so no further dip can happen
The debt sleeve is one part; the other sleeves answer to different drivers
Rate hikes always lift gold and equity, so the fund will gain in the next week
The dip proves the fund is unsuited to her, so the adviser must accept the exit
why: No fund can hedge away all rate risk. A longer-duration sleeve still dips when yields rise.
Sleeves respond to different drivers, and the debt dip is a fraction of a 30% sleeve. Exiting turns a paper dip real.
Rate hikes do not always lift gold or equity. The sleeves have their own drivers, not a fixed response.
A small dip does not show unsuitability. Suitability rests on her goals and horizon, not a single week.

pts: A rate hike dips bond prices first (about duration times the rise in yields) and then raises accrual. The dip is mark to market, not a permanent loss.
In a multi-asset fund only the debt sleeve feels it directly. Gold and equity answer to their own drivers.
Explain the small NAV wobble before the client sees it, and quote the duration from the factsheet.
